title: The Lesson I Learned From the Fig Tree That Had Leaves But No Fruit
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From the Fig Tree That Had Leaves But No Fruit
(Mark 11:13)
It looked alive from a distance.
That’s what shook me.

Jesus saw a fig tree covered in leaves, full of outward promise, but when He came closer, there was no fruit.
Plenty of appearance.
Zero substance.
A public display of life hiding a private barrenness.
And I felt that.

Because that tree is not just a tree.
Sometimes, that tree is me.

I’ve had seasons where I knew the language of faith, but not the fire of intimacy.
I had the appearance of devotion, but not the evidence of surrender.
I could say the right things, post the right verses, show up in the right places—yet deep inside, God was confronting what people could not see.

Leaves can fool people.
They never fool Jesus.

Mark 11:13 reminds us that Christ does not only inspect what is visible.
He looks for fruit.
Not performance.
Not image.
Fruit.

The fruit of repentance.
The fruit of obedience.
The fruit of love, holiness, humility, and a life transformed by grace.
But here’s what we miss:

This is not just a warning about hypocrisy.
It is also an invitation to honesty.

Because the answer is not to tape fruit onto dead branches.
The answer is to abide in Christ.

Jesus does not call us to fake fullness.
He calls us to remain in Him, because real fruit is never manufactured by religious effort. It is produced by a heart rooted in the Savior.

That fig tree taught me something painful and beautiful:
God is not impressed by my leaves.
He wants my life.

And the good news is this—if you’ve been living leafy but fruitless, Jesus is still merciful.
He exposes what is empty, not to shame you, but to lead you back to the only One who can make you fruitful again.

You do not need a better image.
You need a deeper surrender.

Come back to Christ.
Let Him cleanse what is fake, heal what is dry, and grow what only grace can grow.
From a distance, leaves may look impressive.
But in the Kingdom, fruit is what matters.
“Lord, don’t let me be impressive without being fruitful.”
